group.passage:
New Zealand is famous for its stunning natural landscapes, but early British mapmakers didn’t always show much creativity. They gave dull names like “Mount Horrible” to a tall mountain and “Silly Pool” to a small lake. Over 260 places are named after James Cook, the first European to explore the country.
[[1]] Many locations around the country are being renamed using Te Reo Maori, the language of the indigenous people. Since 2019, over 3,000 Maori names have become official. On June 6th, 2024, the New Zealand Geographic Board started asking the public for feedback on six more name changes. One proposal is to rename “Petone,” a suburb of Wellington, to “Pito One,” which is the area’s original Maori name. Another is to give a name to a part of Auckland’s waterfront: it may become “Te Toangaroa,” a name connected to Maori waka (canoes) that once traveled along the shore.
About 20 percent of the population are Maori, and many others also support the changes. In most cases, the Maori and English names will be used side by side. But pronunciation can be a challenge: a 2021 survey showed that 70% of New Zealanders (also known as Kiwis) could speak only a few words or phrases in Maori. The correct way to say “Maori” is “mao-dee” with a soft “d.” The town Paraparaumu should be pronounced “pada-pada-oo-moo,” but many call it “para-pram” or just “pram.” [[2]]
When New Zealand became a British colony, Maori people and their language were pushed aside. [[3]] One example is Te Umu Kaha, which became “Temuka” in the 1800s. For many years, radio and TV presenters were expected to speak with a British accent called Received Pronunciation (RP). Maori was not made an official language until 1987, even though the country became a dominion in 1907.
Since then, things have improved. Today, more than 9,000 places officially have Maori names, and the language is often heard on television and radio. Many schoolchildren also learn basic Maori. Still, both Maori and non-Maori speakers often say words in unusual ways. This is an example of how languages influence each other when they are spoken together. [[4]] They usually happen slowly. After nearly 200 years of being spoken alongside English, some simple Maori vowels (called monophthongs) have already changed over time.

options_bank.A: At that time, signs and newspapers were only in English, and many Maori words were changed or shortened.
options_bank.B: In linguistics, these kinds of changes are known as “contact phenomena.”
options_bank.C: There would be no changes to addresses or any need to update road signs.
options_bank.D: Today, there are efforts to replace some simple or old-fashioned names with more meaningful and poetic ones.
options_bank.E: Whangarei, a city in the north, should be said as “farng-ah-rey,” but people often say “wang-a-ray” instead.

tags.topic: restoring Maori place names in New Zealand
